angle: You can research 50,000 accounts in under an hour with AI signals
post_first_line: 50,000 accounts researched in under an hour.
linkedin_post:
50,000 accounts researched in under an hour.

That's the part of AI signals that changes how a GTM team works.

You can do research on 50,000 accounts in less than an hour and outreach to all of them, or queue them up for your sales team to go after.

But the speed isn't what I find most useful.

It's that you can see what the AI is doing. You can see what it's searching for, the different sites it's going after, and the different tools it's using. The primary one is internet search.

That auditability matters. The AI piece isn't really a black box.

If your reps can't see where a signal came from, they won't trust it. If they don't trust it, they won't act on it.

Speed gets the research done. Transparency gets it used.

Slide 4: The quieter win is seeing what the AI searches

lesson.title: Auditable AI research beats black-box research
takeaways: AI can research 50,000 accounts in less than an hour, then feed outreach or your sales team's queue.
Being able to see which sites and tools the AI uses, like internet search, builds trust in the output.
The AI piece shouldn't be a black box, because auditability is what lets a team act on the research.
lesson.exercise: Pick one AI-generated account research output your team uses today. Trace where each signal came from (which site or tool). If you can't trace it, write down what you'd need to see before a rep would confidently act on it.

angle: 30 meetings in one month from signals tailored to your ICP instead of generic intent
post_first_line: Generic intent data is not enough.
linkedin_post:
Generic intent data is not enough.

A few months ago, we started leaning into custom AI signals.

The idea is simple. We check a segment of our TAM, something like 40,000 accounts, for signals that are specific to our ICP.

Product launches are a good example. When an account launches a product, we call it out directly in the email copy. One of our replies came straight from that signal.

This is different from a new hire alert or website intent. Those are useful. But this one is tailored to our business.

Here's how we build them:

We work backwards from what we would send manually, one-to-one. We look at the research we would do by hand. Then we figure out how to scale it.

The signal isn't the point. The point is turning your best manual outreach into something that runs across your whole TAM.

Start with what you would send to one account if you had unlimited time. Then build the system to do that at scale.

Slide 2: We built custom AI signals around our own business
Slide 3: We check a segment of our TAM, like 40,000 accounts
Slide 4: One signal we track: product launches
Slide 5: We call the launch out directly in the email copy
Slide 6: New hire and website intent are fine, but not tailored
Slide 7: Work backwards from what you'd send one-to-one
Slide 8: Then scale that research across your whole TAM

lesson.title: Build signals from your manual outreach, not from a vendor list
takeaways: Custom AI signals can be tailored to your ICP in a way generic intent can't.
A signal like a product launch can be referenced directly in the email copy.
Start from what you would send one-to-one, then scale that research.
lesson.exercise: Pick one account you'd love to land. Write down the research you'd do and the first line you'd send by hand. Turn that research into one signal you could check across a segment of your TAM.

caption: Stop relying on generic intent

angle: We expanded our product launch signal from 7 to 30 days after it started booking meetings
post_first_line: Our best signal started as a 7-day window.
linkedin_post:
Our best signal started as a 7-day window.

The signal: has this company launched a major new product recently? If yes, return the product name.

We started off with the last 7 days. It was a big success.

Then we booked more and more meetings through it, so we doubled down and expanded it to 30 days.

The product name it returns is what makes it work. We then use it in the email copy, so the outreach references something real about the prospect.

The lesson: when a signal books meetings, don't leave it alone. Widen the window and see how much more it can catch.

Start narrow, prove it works, then expand.

lesson.title: Expand the signals that book meetings
takeaways: Start with a tight time window, then widen it once the signal proves itself.
Let meeting results tell you which signals deserve more investment.
Return a specific data point, like the product name, so the email copy can use it.
lesson.exercise: Pick the one signal in your outbound that has booked the most meetings. Check its time window, widen it, and compare meetings booked before and after.

angle: How we found our best signal by analyzing closed-won transcripts instead of guessing
post_first_line: Our ICP wasn't what we assumed.
linkedin_post:
Our ICP wasn't what we assumed.

We thought we knew our top segments. Pretty standard, the businesses we sell into.

Then we looked back at our closed-won customers and ran the conversation transcripts through conversational intelligence.

We weren't reading for vibes. We were looking for particular moments.

One of them: a recent product launch. If a company had one, they were looking at Unify at a higher clip.

Then industry. Looking back at closed-won, we had a disproportionate number of fintech companies.

Nobody on the team had called that out. It only showed up when we looked at the data.

Most teams build their signals from gut feel and a whiteboard. The better source is already sitting in your call recordings.

Your closed-won deals are telling you who buys and why. Most of us just never go back and listen.

Slide 8: Your best signals are already in your call recordings.

lesson.title: Mine closed-won transcripts for signals, don't guess them
takeaways: Your assumed ICP and your actual ICP can differ. Closed-won data shows the gap.
Look for particular moments in transcripts, like a recent product launch, instead of only firmographics.
Industry patterns can hide in plain sight: we found a disproportionate number of fintech companies.
lesson.exercise: Pull your last closed-won customers and their call transcripts. List the moments and industries that repeat across them, then compare that list to your current ICP definition.

caption: Stop guessing your ICP

angle: Why 95% accuracy in AI outreach is better than 100% manual
linkedin_post:
Perfect outreach doesn't exist.

When we launch an AI outreach agent, I delay the sequence first. You can do this natively in Unify.

Then I read the emails and check the accuracy. I'm making sure it's not doing anything wacky.

If a reply comes in saying "we didn't launch this product," or the reference is from X months ago, I tweak the agent and keep testing.

And yes, there will be edge cases. We'll probably get one every few thousand.

It's well worth it, based on the success.

Zooming out, it's not going to be 100% perfect. But if it's 95% to 98% accurate, that makes complete sense, especially in terms of ROI.

Most teams stall because they're chasing a standard that manual outreach never met either.

The real question isn't whether the agent makes mistakes. It's whether you catch the pattern, fix the agent, and keep shipping.

Delay. Audit. Tweak. Repeat.
carousel: Slide 1: 100% accurate AI outreach is a myth worth dropping
Slide 2: Launch the sequence delayed, never straight to send
Slide 3: Read the emails and check for anything wacky
Slide 4: A reply says wrong product? Tweak the agent, keep testing
Slide 5: Edge cases happen. Probably one every few thousand
Slide 6: 95% to 98% accurate makes complete sense for ROI
Slide 7: Delay. Audit. Tweak. Repeat. Then let it run

lesson.title: Ship AI outreach at 95%, not never at 100%
takeaways: Delay the sequence at launch so you can check every email's accuracy before anything sends.
Treat bad replies as feedback: tweak the agent and keep testing instead of scrapping it.
Edge cases are the cost of doing business. At 95% to 98% accuracy, the ROI still makes complete sense.
lesson.exercise: Set up your next AI outreach sequence with a send delay. Review the drafted emails, list every error type you spot, and update your agent's instructions to fix the top one before launch.

caption: 95% accurate beats never shipping

angle: First-party intent still works, but only if you're not competing with 50 other reps using the same signal
linkedin_post:
Pricing page visits still convert.

The angle here is that first-party intent still works. But the transcript only supports part of that story, so I'll stick to what we actually see.

If someone's already on your website showing high intent on the pricing page, that's a very successful signal for us still.

Last month, over 20 meetings just from website intent and prospecting within those accounts.

First-party signals aren't just pricing page views. They include:

- MQLs from gated content
- Product tour views
- CRM data
- Close lost opportunities, based on the loss reason

Then there are third-party signals, which are getting extremely popular:

- Social signals, like people engaging with Austin's (our CEO) LinkedIn posts
- People engaging with Unify on LinkedIn
- Potentially competitor engagement on LinkedIn
- Job openings, like a new sales leader or a new marketing hire

The signal list is easy to build. The harder part is deciding which signals you trust enough to act on.

For us, the one that keeps working is the person already on our site, looking at pricing.

Which signal is quietly carrying your pipeline right now?

lesson.title: Stack first-party and third-party signals
takeaways: A visit to the pricing page is still a very successful signal for us.
First-party signals include gated content MQLs, product tour views, CRM data and close lost reasons.
Third-party signals include LinkedIn engagement, competitor engagement and job openings like new sales or marketing hires.
lesson.exercise: List every signal you currently act on and tag each one first-party or third-party. Then pull last month's meetings and note which signal sourced each one. Double down on the top signal and cut the ones that sourced nothing.
